completedPhaseClaims.summary: Reliability, flakiness, resource and operational-soundness pass over the delivered namespace-lock harness. Verdict UNSTABLE, qualified: no active instability was measured (all four TestNamespaceLock_ guards PASS, nslock package 0.214s, integration-light lane exit 0), and the label is not PARTIALLY_STABLE only because the two substantive findings require authoring a test, which is bubbles.test's artifact rather than stabilize's. ST-1 (MEDIUM): the release path has no guard, and no test written against the current callers could give it one, because every caller registers t.Cleanup(pool.Close) before Acquire registers the unlock, so closing the pool releases the lock whether or not pg_advisory_unlock worked -- a working unlock and a broken one produce the same observable. The package doc names a leaked lock (a HUNG suite) as the worst design outcome, and that is the one property nothing tests. ST-2 (MEDIUM): the LIFO backstop that bounds a failed unlock to one test is a caller convention, not a package property, and callsite_contract_test.go enforces the Acquire call but not the pool-close ordering; ST-1 and ST-2 compound under a TestMain-scoped pool, which is the ordinary optimisation that relaxing -p 1 would motivate. ST-3 (LOW-MEDIUM): acquireTimeout 60s is not budgeted against go test -timeout 300s; the largest acquiring package has 4 acquire points (240s worst case), so a fifth reaches the package timeout and replaces the helper's addressed t.Fatalf with a goroutine-dump panic exactly when contention becomes real. ST-4 (LOW, latent): a second Acquire on one *testing.T pins a different pooled connection, so it self-deadlocks for 60s; unreachable today but resetKnowledgeStatsTables acquires from inside a helper taking t, which is the shape that eventually gets called twice. ST-5/ST-6 informational: ABBA deadlock is impossible with one locked namespace and the 60s bound would convert any future one into a bounded named failure; there is no runtime cliff under -p 1, and the cliff is conditional on relaxing it. ST-7: a hypothesised defect was REFUTED by measurement rather than shipped.

executionHistory.note: Reliability and operational-soundness diagnosis of the delivered namespace-lock harness. Nothing was mutated: no test authored, no source file changed, no probe created, so no restore was needed and no `trap ... EXIT` was used anywhere. Measured this phase: all four TestNamespaceLock_ guards PASS with the nslock package at 0.214s and the whole integration-light lane at exit 0; the lane passes `-p 1 -tags integration -v -count=1 -timeout 300s` while the helper's acquireTimeout is 60s, and the two constants live in different files with neither referencing the other; acquire points per package are nslock 4, openknowledge 3, e2e/openknowledge 2, integration 1, selfknowledge 1; every caller registers t.Cleanup(pool.Close) inside its pool helper before Acquire, so LIFO does put the unlock first as the package doc claims; the lane hardcodes -count=1 and exposes only --go-run, so no zero-mutation in-process release probe was available and none was manufactured. Seven findings, all ROUTED rather than fixed, because each needs a test or lane-script change owned by another agent. The load-bearing one is ST-1: release is the single property no guard asserts, and it is not merely untested but structurally unobservable through the current callers, since pool.Close would release the lock whether or not pg_advisory_unlock worked -- so a broken unlock and a working one produce the same result. ST-2 shows the LIFO backstop is a caller convention that callsite_contract_test.go does not enforce, and the two compound under a TestMain-scoped pool. ST-3 quantifies the unbudgeted 60s-vs-300s timeout relationship at one acquire of headroom. ST-4 records a bounded 60s self-deadlock on a double acquire, unreachable today but latent because an acquiring helper takes t. ST-7 is a hypothesis this phase raised and then refuted by measurement against a live PostgreSQL rather than shipping: negative FNV keys do NOT break IsHeld, because int8shl wraps instead of raising, and the exclusion guard in fact exercises the harder negative-key case. The packet's residual is unchanged and was not re-litigated: F4 remains open and no finding here touches it, because F4 is production code that never takes the test-side lock.

notes: Pre-existing defect, not introduced by this session's commits.

A1 (audit): scripts/runtime/go-integration.sh passes `-p 1`; no contending file calls t.Parallel(); the go/python lanes are sequential docker runs. The two packages never run concurrently, so the documented interleaving was unreachable during the original red.
The landed lock is DEFENCE-IN-DEPTH: it makes exclusion a property of the namespace rather than of a flag in a shell script, and covers a future `-p >1` or a shared-DB cross-lane run.

F4 is the primary remaining hypothesis: internal/assistant/selfknowledge/ingestor.go deletes every smackerel_self row whose content_hash is absent from the corpus, which is every row these tests insert. It runs at core boot, and the core container is not serialised by -p 1.
The production stale sweep itself is designed behaviour and is unchanged.
